title: Battle map grid & generation from a POI
summary: The square grid every tactical battle is fought on: cells with a terrain kind, height, cover value and hit points, made from the POI the team raids (slice: one simple building template stamped into a small yard), with spawn, container and extraction zones.
whyHere: It opens the combat lane: turns, pathing, LOS, actions and the AI all read and write the BattleMap, so it must exist (and be testable headless) before any of them. It needs the POI and loot cards to know what is being raided.
subsystems: Cell kinds table (walk / cover / blocks sight)
sliceScope: One map size (about 32 × 24). One building template from JSON (a house: 3–4 rooms, inner doors, 1 front door, a few windows) stamped in the middle of a yard with fences, cars and trees for cover. 3–6 containers from gear.loot, a deploy zone on one edge, an extraction zone at the same edge, the dead placed 14–20 tiles from the team. Same seed + same POI = same map.
fullScope: battlesize.js: four size classes 24×18 to 48×34, raids 32×24 to 56×42 by site type, real-size buildings up to 300–500 cells a side; buildingmaps.js archetypes split footprints into rooms (L/T/U shapes, 12 named plans a kind, storeys and stairs), 248 furniture kinds, densify tops up cover until most open ground has cover within 3 tiles.

data: content/battle/cells.json: each cell kind's walk, cover (0 none, 1 half, 2 full), blocksSight, hp, moveCost, artKey (open, wall, door, window, fence, car, tree, crate)
content/battle/templates/house_small.json: a char-grid template ('#' wall, 'D' door, 'W' window, 'C' container slot, '.' floor) with room tags for loot
BattleSize record (w, h, contactRange [14,20], coverRadius 3) per context in content/battle/sizes.json
Validation test: every template is enclosed, every room reachable from the front door, every container slot on floor
backend: BattleMap class: flat Cell[] of w*h, Idx(x,y)=y*w+x, InBounds, neighbours (4 and 8), a Revision counter bumped on any cell change (for caches)
MapGenerator.Generate(BattleSetup, Rng) → yard scatter, stamp template, place containers, zones; seed = hash(worldSeed, tileId, poiId) so revisits match
Zones: deploy cells, extraction mask (bool[]), enemy spawn cells; reachability flood-fill check (regenerate or knock a door if a zone is cut off)
Unit tests: determinism (same seed → identical cell hash), reachability, counts of containers and dead within bounds
ui: BattleView draws cells with placeholder diamonds/colour blocks by artKey via the ArtCatalog; GridToScreen / ScreenToGrid helpers for clicks
Debug overlay toggle: cell coords, zones, cover values

connections.why: the POI picked on the State Map decides the template, size and loot theme
connections.how: BattleSetup carries PoiId; MapGenerator reads PoiDef.TemplateId and LootTableId from ContentDb
connections.godot: SimHost starts the battle and changes to Battle.tscn; the scene asks SimHost for the BattleMap
connections.unity: SimHost loads the Battle scene (LoadSceneAsync) and hands it the BattleMap

connections.why: cover and sight are read straight off the cell kinds and heights
connections.how: CellDef.Cover / BlocksSight looked up by Cell.Kind; LOS cache keyed by BattleMap.Revision
connections.godot: nothing engine-side: pure sim

connections.why: the battle view draws this grid isometrically
connections.how: the view reads Cells and listens to CellChanged(x,y) events (a door opened, a wall broken)
connections.godot: TileMapLayer with an isometric TileSet, cells set from artKey; signal CellChanged → SetCell
connections.unity: Tilemap on a Grid with Isometric cell layout; SetTile per cell; C# event CellChanged

connections.why: containers on the map are filled from loot tables
connections.how: Container { Id, X, Y, LootTableId, Searched }; contents rolled lazily on first search with the battle Rng
connections.godot: container sprite node per container, highlighted when searchable
connections.unity: container prefab per container, highlighted when searchable

godot.approach: Keep the grid in C# (BattleMap) and only mirror it into a TileMapLayer whose TileSet uses the isometric tile shape. Convert with your own GridToScreen so clicks map back to sim cells (or TileMapLayer.LocalToMap). Walls and props that must sort with units go on a Y-sorted Node2D layer rather than the floor TileMapLayer.

unity.approach: A Grid with Cell Layout 'Isometric Z As Y' and a Tilemap for the floor; tall things (walls, units) sorted by a Custom Axis sort or as SpriteRenderers. The sim's BattleMap stays the truth: the Tilemap is rebuilt from it and GridLayout.WorldToCell turns a mouse click into (x, y).

newb: Logic is a plain square grid; isometric is only how you draw it. Screen = ((x − y) · tileW/2, (x + y) · tileH/2). Never store screen positions in the sim.
A flat array indexed y*W+x is faster and simpler to save than a 2-D array of objects; every other system (pathing, LOS caches) uses that index.
Generating from a seed means you never save the map for a revisit: same seed, same building. You only save what changed (doors broken, containers searched).
Templates as ASCII grids in JSON are a great first 'level editor': readable, diffable, and a test can check them.
A Revision counter on the map is a cheap way to tell caches 'something changed, throw yourself away'.
pitfalls: Mixing up iso screen coordinates and grid coordinates in game logic (bugs that only appear on diagonals).
Using the engine's TileMap as the data: it ties your rules to one engine and cannot run in dotnet test.
Generating a map where the deploy zone cannot reach the building or the exit: always flood-fill check.
Using System.Random or GD.Randi in the generator: maps stop being reproducible.
test: xUnit: same seed produces the same cell hash; every template room is reachable; containers and the dead land on walkable cells; zones are not cut off. Manual: open the battle from a POI twice, see the identical house, click cells and see the debug overlay show the right (x, y).

title: Turn order, action points & battle state machine
summary: The battle's flow as an explicit state machine (Setup → Deploy → PlayerTurn → EnemyTurn → … → Over) with XCOM-style 2 action points per unit per turn, start/end-of-turn hooks and a win/lose check after every action.
whyHere: Every action, the AI and the battle UI need to know whose turn it is and what a unit can still do; this is the spine the other combat cards hang on, right after the map exists.
sliceScope: Phases: Setup, PlayerTurn, EnemyTurn, Over. Every unit gets 2 AP at its side's turn start; moving within 1 move range costs 1 AP, a dash (up to 2× range) costs 2; shooting, overwatch-free 'hunker' and extract end the unit's turn. End Turn button. The enemy phase runs one unit per Step() so the UI can animate each. End check after each action: all dead gone → victory, no active survivors → defeat (or retreat if any extracted).
fullScope: combat.js runs player / enemy / third-side phases with a deploy phase for base defence, ~25 start/end-of-turn hooks (bleeding out after 3 turns, stuns, fire, acid, tunnels, Heat 1.2 a turn plus noise bringing a wave every 25), surprised units starting with 0 AP, and 'area clear enough' early endings on big maps (battlesize CLEAR: at most 2 far, unaware stragglers).

data: BattleRules record in content/battle/rules.json: apPerTurn 2, bleedTurns 3, heatPerTurn 1.2, heatStage 25
BattlePhase enum and BattleEvent types (TurnStarted, PhaseChanged, UnitActed, UnitDied, BattleEnded)
Battle runtime class (map, units, phase, turn, rng, log) as plain serialisable data
backend: BattleStateMachine: Enter/Exit per phase, a single Advance() that moves Setup→PlayerTurn, EndTurn() → EnemyTurn, last enemy done → PlayerTurn (turn++)
Turn hooks as an ordered list of ITurnHook (OnSideTurnStart / OnSideTurnEnd) so later cards (bleeding, Heat, stealth) plug in without editing the core
EnemyStep(): pop the next unit from the queue, run its AI, check end, return the unit (or null when the phase is over)
CheckEnd() after every command and every enemy step; set Outcome and enter Over exactly once
Tests: AP spent and refreshed, enemy queue order deterministic, end detected, no commands accepted outside PlayerTurn
ui: Turn banner ('Your turn' / 'The dead move'), AP pips on each unit, End Turn button and hotkey
During EnemyTurn the view calls Step(), waits for the move animation, then calls Step() again

connections.why: actions spend AP and are only legal in PlayerTurn
connections.how: IBattleCommand.Validate checks Phase == PlayerTurn and unit.Ap ≥ cost; Execute subtracts AP then calls CheckEnd()
connections.godot: action bar buttons send commands through SimHost.Battle.Do(cmd)
connections.unity: action bar buttons send commands through SimHost.Battle.Do(cmd)

connections.why: the enemy phase is the AI's turn, one unit at a time
connections.how: EnemyStep() calls IUnitBrain.TakeTurn(battle, unit) for the unit popped from EnemyQueue
connections.godot: a Battle scene script awaits the animation (await ToSignal(tween, Tween.SignalName.Finished)) between steps
connections.unity: a coroutine or async Awaitable loop yields until the move animation ends between steps

connections.why: a battle pauses the campaign clock
connections.how: Battle start publishes BattleStarted; the clock's Paused flag is held by a 'battle' pause reason until BattleEnded
connections.godot: SimHost stops ticking the campaign in _Process while Battle != null
connections.unity: SimHost stops ticking the campaign in Update while Battle != null

connections.why: the view shows phase, turn and AP
connections.how: BattleEvent queue drained each frame by the bridge (PhaseChanged, UnitActed)
connections.godot: SimHost re-emits as C# [Signal] delegates (PhaseChanged, UnitActed)

godot.approach: The state machine lives in the sim; the Battle scene only reacts. Drive the enemy phase from an async method: call Step(), play that unit's tween, await its Finished signal, repeat. Keep a 'busy' flag so input is ignored while the enemy acts.

unity.approach: Same sim state machine; a BattleController MonoBehaviour runs the enemy phase in a coroutine (or async Awaitable method), stepping the sim and yielding until each unit's walk finishes. Input is disabled while it runs.

newb: A state machine is just 'the battle is always in exactly one named phase, and only certain transitions are allowed'. Writing it as an enum + one switch kills a whole class of 'it is both turns at once' bugs.
Action points make choices legible: 2 AP = move+move, move+shoot, or dash. Shooting ending the turn (XCOM rule, also the prototype's) stops 'shoot, shoot, run away'.
The sim must never wait for animations. It resolves instantly; the view replays events at its own pace. Stepping the enemy phase one unit at a time is how you get both.
Hooks (start/end of turn) let later features (bleeding, Heat, fire) add rules without touching the core loop: open for extension, closed for edits.
pitfalls: Putting turn logic in the scene script: it then cannot be tested or reused by auto-resolve and the autopilot.
Forgetting to re-check victory after a kill in the enemy phase (a zombie killing the last survivor must end the battle there).
Letting the player click during the enemy phase and send commands mid-step.
Iterating the unit list while units are added (screamer calls, waves) or removed: copy the queue of IDs first.
test: xUnit: a scripted battle (1 survivor, 1 walker) runs Setup→Player→Enemy→Player with AP 2→0→2; commands are refused outside PlayerTurn; killing the last enemy sets Outcome=Victory once; the enemy queue order is the same for the same seed. Manual: end turn, watch each dead walk in turn, banner flips back.

title: Tactical grid pathfinding & movement costs
summary: How units move on the battle grid: a Dijkstra flood for the 'where can I go with my AP' highlight and path, movement costs from terrain, doors and vaulting, and one shared flow field the whole crowd of the dead walks down toward the team.
whyHere: Needed by both the Move action and the dead's chase; it only needs the map and AP rules, and the AI is far cheaper to write once flow fields exist.
subsystems: Flow / distance field for the dead
sliceScope: 8-direction movement, diagonals 1.5, no cutting past a wall corner, units block cells. Reachable(unit, budget) = Dijkstra out to 2 × move (5 tiles a person, 3 a walker, 6 a runner) giving cost and 'prev' per cell; PathTo(x, y) walks prev back. A DistanceField from the team's cells (Dijkstra over the whole map, ignoring units) that each dead unit follows downhill. Closed doors cost 1 to open for people; the dead batter doors at cost 2 + 0.4 × hp.
fullScope: combat.js reachable / distField: heights only change on stairs or ladders, climbs cost per level (×1.5 in rain, ×2.5 in winter), vaulting half cover +2 and lands winded, mud +0.5, snow +0.25, acid avoided by weight, tunnels as links, fire closed to people; siege fields let the dead pile on the weakest door; fields are cached (8 per key) and patched after a door is hit so a 500 × 500 map with 100 dead stays under 1.5 s a turn.

data: Move costs on CellDef (moveCost, passable, vaultable) and on unit defs (mob tiles per AP)
MoveRules record: diagonalCost 1.5, vaultCost 2, doorBashBase 2, doorBashPerHp 0.4
backend: Pathfinder.Reachable(battle, unit, maxCost) → ReachResult { float[] Cost; int[] Prev } using .NET PriorityQueue<int,float>
PathTo(ReachResult, x, y) and MoveCost; Move command charges 1 AP if cost ≤ mob else 2
DistanceField.Build(map, sources, walkerProfile) → float[]; NextStep(field, x, y) picks the lowest neighbour that is free
FieldCache keyed by (map.Revision, profile, sources hash) so 20 dead in a turn share one field
Optional A*(start, goal) with octile heuristic for single long queries (an NPC going to a specific door)
Tests: corner cutting refused, costs of known paths, blocked cells, field gradient always reaches a source
ui: Move-range overlay: cells with cost ≤ mob tinted one colour, ≤ 2·mob another (dash)
Path preview line from the selected unit to the hovered cell, with the AP it will cost

connections.why: Move uses the reachable set and the path, step by step
connections.how: MoveCommand validates target in Reachable(...).Cost ≤ unit dash range, then walks PathTo cell by cell (each step can trigger overwatch / noise)
connections.godot: the view plays UnitMoved(id, path[]) as a Tween along GridToScreen points
connections.unity: the view plays UnitMoved(id, path[]) with a coroutine lerping along CellToWorld points

connections.why: the dead chase by the flow field; humans pick cells from the reachable set
connections.how: ZombieBrain asks FieldCache.For(team cells, Dead) and steps downhill; human utility scoring iterates ReachResult cells
connections.godot: pure sim

connections.why: a door broken or wall knocked down must invalidate fields
connections.how: BattleMap.Revision++ on every cell change; caches compare revision
connections.godot: pure sim

connections.why: big maps (300–500 a side) need incremental field patching later
connections.how: keep the field API stable so a patching implementation can replace the full rebuild
connections.godot: can run field builds on a worker via Task.Run in the sim
connections.unity: can move field builds into the Job System later

godot.approach: Write the pathfinder in the engine-free sim (it must run in dotnet test and in auto-resolve). Godot's AStarGrid2D is handy for a throwaway prototype but cannot express vault costs, doors that the dead batter, or flow fields, so do not build on it. The engine only draws the overlay and tweens the walk.

unity.approach: NavMesh is for continuous 3-D worlds, not turn-based grids: skip it and use the sim's own Dijkstra. Draw the move range on an overlay Tilemap and the path with a LineRenderer. If fields get slow on huge maps later, the Job System + Burst can run the same algorithm over NativeArrays.

learn.t: Flow field pathfinding for many units

newb: Dijkstra floods outward from one start and gives the cost to every cell: exactly what the blue 'you can move here' area needs. A* is Dijkstra with a hint toward one goal: best for one path, useless for an area.
Flow field: run one Dijkstra from the targets (your team) outward; now every cell knows its distance. Each of 40 dead just steps to its cheapest neighbour. One search instead of 40 A* runs.
Costs are where gameplay lives: vaulting a fence for +2, mud for +0.5, a door the dead must batter for 2 + 0.4 × hp. Same algorithm, different weights.
No corner cutting means a diagonal step is only allowed if both orthogonal neighbours are passable, so nobody slips through a wall's corner.
Store 'prev' per cell during the search; the path is just following prev back from the goal.
pitfalls: Using a List and sorting it every pop: fine on 32 × 24, a disaster on 300 × 300. Use PriorityQueue.
Letting the flow field treat units as walls: then a crowd blocks its own field. Ignore units in the field, check occupancy only on the actual step.
Floating-point diagonal costs (1.5) compared with == : always compare with a small epsilon.
Rebuilding the field for every zombie instead of caching per revision.
test: xUnit: on hand-made 5 × 5 maps, known costs (straight 4 = 4, diagonal 2 = 3), corner cutting blocked, occupied cells excluded as destinations, flow field strictly decreases toward the team, cache reused when revision unchanged and rebuilt after a door breaks. Manual: hover cells and check the AP shown matches the walk.

title: Line of sight, cover & hit chance
summary: Who can see whom (lines traced across the grid, heights, sight ranges, fog of war), how much cover a target has against a given shooter (from the cells on its four sides), and the hit-chance formula with a readable breakdown the UI shows.
whyHere: Shooting, overwatch, the dead noticing you and the fog of war all depend on it; it sits after the map and before actions so 'shoot' can be validated and its odds shown.
subsystems: Field of view & fog of war (shadowcasting)
sliceScope: Los(a, b): walk the cells on the line between centres; a sight-blocking cell blocks, ignoring start and end. Sight 13 tiles for people, 9 for the dead. Fog of war = union of what your units see this turn. Cover: each of the target's 4 neighbour cells gives 0/1/2; it counts only if the shooter is in front of that side. Hit% = aim + weapon aim − range falloff − cover (0/20/40) + 15 if target unaware, clamped 5–95; crit 25% if exposed, 10% vs the dead, 5% in cover, ×2 damage.
fullScope: combat.js los samples the line 4× a tile with corner grazing and heights (eye 0.6 above the cell), caches every pair (dense Int8Array to 5000 cells, sparse Map after); hollows shut sight, high ground +2 sight and +5 aim a level (max +15), full cover from 2 levels up; night cones (vision.js 120°, 4–7 tiles dark), fog −4, smoke; shotOdds has ~20 labelled rows (range, round drop, bipod, hunker −20, reaction −15, flank, height).

data: SightRules: personSight 13, deadSight 9, nightSight 7 / dead 5 (post-slice)
CoverRules: coverPenalty [0, 20, 40], frontDot 0.35, hunker 20, unawareBonus 15, reactionPenalty 15, hit clamp 5..95
Weapon aim fields used here: aim, optimalRange, falloffPerTile, crit bonus (from gear.weapons)
backend: Los.Clear(map, x0,y0, x1,y1): supercover line (every cell the segment touches), symmetric, cached by (a,b) and map.Revision
Fov.Compute(map, x, y, range) with symmetric shadowcasting for the fog of war; Battle.Visible[side] bitset updated after each move
Cover.Against(map, tx,ty, sx,sy) → {Level, Flanked}: max cover over the 4 sides whose direction · (shooter − target)/dist > 0.35; flanked = some cover nearby but none facing
HitChance.Shot(battle, shooter, target) → ShotOdds { Chance, Crit, DmgMin, DmgMax, List<(string label, int delta)> Parts }
Tests: wall blocks, door open/closed, symmetric LOS, cover facing vs flanked, each formula row with fixed numbers
ui: Fog of war overlay (unseen cells dimmed, last-seen enemies as ghosts)
Cover shields on cell edges when hovering a cell (half / full, from CoverSides)
Target hover shows hit % and the breakdown list ('Half cover −20', 'Range −6')

connections.why: Shoot needs LOS and rolls against the chance; overwatch fires when a mover enters a visible cell
connections.how: ShootCommand.Validate calls Los/CanSee; Execute rolls battle.Rng.Next(100) < odds.Chance
connections.godot: target hover calls SimHost.Battle.Odds(a,t) and shows the Parts list in a tooltip Control
connections.unity: target hover calls SimHost.Battle.Odds(a,t) and shows Parts in a UI Toolkit tooltip

connections.why: the dead notice by sight; human AI scores cells by cover and flank
connections.how: AI calls CanSee and Cover.Against for candidate cells; same functions as the player (AI parity, ADR 0001)
connections.godot: pure sim

connections.why: fog, shields and odds are the battle's most read information
connections.how: Battle.Visible[Player] bitset + VisibilityChanged event; CoverSides(x,y) → int[4]
connections.godot: a CanvasItem _Draw over the TileMapLayer, or a fog TileMapLayer
connections.unity: a fog Tilemap layer tinted per cell, shields as small sprites

connections.why: post-slice: vision cones, darkness and sneaking extend CanSee
connections.how: CanSee(a,t) is the one gate; stealth adds rules inside it (cone, light, sneak behind cover)
connections.godot: pure sim

godot.approach: All of this is sim math: do not use physics raycasts (RayCast2D) for game rules, they depend on colliders and frame timing. Godot only draws: a fog layer, edge shields and a tooltip with the breakdown.

unity.approach: Same: no Physics2D.Raycast for rules. A second Tilemap tinted dark for fog, small shield sprites on hovered cell edges, and a UI Toolkit tooltip listing the ShotOdds parts.

newb: Bresenham picks one cell per column, so a line can slip diagonally between two wall cells; a 'supercover' line includes every cell the segment touches and is fairer for walls. The prototype samples 4 points a tile and lets a line graze a corner.
LOS answers 'can A see B?'; FOV (shadowcasting) answers 'what can A see?' in one pass. Use FOV for fog of war, LOS for a single shot.
Make LOS symmetric (A sees B ⇔ B sees A), or players will be shot by things they cannot see.
Cover is directional: a wall east of you protects only against shooters to the east. The dot product of the side's direction with the direction to the shooter tells you if that side faces them.
Return the hit chance as a list of labelled rows, not one number: the UI tooltip, balance tests and your own debugging all read it.
pitfalls: Showing one hit % and rolling with another (UI and sim computing separately): always call the same function.
Rolling RNG inside the odds function: then just hovering a target changes the future. Compute odds without dice; roll only in Execute.
Not caching LOS: fog of war recomputed for every unit every step gets slow fast.
Forgetting that the dead ignore cover rules for themselves (shots at the dead in the prototype get no cover penalty).
test: xUnit: a wall between two units blocks both ways; open door sees, closed does not; half cover facing gives −20, the same cover from behind gives 0 and Flanked=true; range falloff numbers; clamp at 5 and 95; Parts sum to Chance before clamping. Manual: walk round a crate and watch the shields and hit % change.

title: Move, shoot, melee, reload, search, extract
summary: The things a survivor can do on their turn, each a command with validation (a plain-English refusal), an AP cost, its effect and the events it emits: move, shoot, melee, reload, hunker, open door, search a container, extract and sound the retreat.
whyHere: With turns, paths and LOS in place the battle becomes playable; the AI then uses the very same commands, and resolve reads what they recorded (ammo spent, loot carried).
sliceScope: Move (1 AP within move range, 2 AP dash), Shoot (needs LOS and a round in the magazine; ends the turn), Melee (adjacent, 10–95%), Reload (1 AP from the survivor's own ammo), Hunker (+20 defence, ends turn), Open/close door (1 AP), Search container (1 AP, contents into the search window), Extract (standing in the extraction zone: unit leaves with what it carries), Sound the retreat. Every gunshot makes noise that wakes the dead within a radius. Downed at 0 hp, bleeding out in 3 turns.
fullScope: combat.js combatAct handles ~90 action types (overwatch, suppress, throw, vault, shove, drag, tie up, takedowns, medics, vehicles, turrets, windows, barricades, quick search that is free but loud: Heat +5, wakes the unaware within 7 tiles). Damage by weapon range × multipliers, crit ×2, armour classes, physical rounds per magazine, jams up to 12% (gunfire.js).

data: Command records: Move(unitId,x,y), Shoot(unitId,targetId), Melee, Reload, Hunker, Door(x,y), Search(containerId), Extract, Retreat, EndTurn
Action costs and noise radii in content/battle/actions.json (shot noise by weapon, door 3, search 0 in slice)
BattleEvent payloads: UnitMoved(path), ShotFired(hit, dmg, crit), UnitDowned, ContainerOpened, UnitExtracted
backend: IBattleCommand { string? Refusal(Battle); void Execute(Battle) }; Battle.Do(cmd) = refusal or execute + CheckEnd
Move walks the path step by step (so overwatch and noticing can interrupt later); Shoot: odds from combat.los, roll, damage roll, crit, emit events, spend round
Damage → Hp; at 0 → Down with BleedTurns 3; at bleed 0 → Dead; the dead die outright
Search: roll the container's loot table once (battle Rng), move chosen items into the unit's carried inventory (gear.items rules, weight)
Extract / Retreat: mark units Extracted, they leave the map with their carried items; when none active remain, the battle ends
Tests per command: each refusal string, AP spent, ammo spent, loot moved, noise wakes the right dead
ui: Action bar for the selected unit (buttons + hotkeys) with greyed buttons showing the refusal as a tooltip
Search window: container contents on one side, the survivor's inventory on the other (reuses ui.inventory)
Floating text for hits/misses/damage; combat log lines

connections.why: the dead and enemy humans act through the same commands
connections.how: brains build IBattleCommand objects and call Battle.Do; ADR 0001 parity means no AI-only shortcuts
connections.godot: pure sim

connections.why: shots read the weapon's aim, damage, magazine and calibre
connections.how: Unit.WeaponId → WeaponDef in ContentDb; Unit.MagRounds spent per shot; Reload draws matching rounds from the unit's inventory
connections.godot: magazine count label from UnitChanged event
connections.unity: magazine count label from UnitChanged event

connections.why: every action plays as animation and log
connections.how: events appended to Battle.Events; bridge drains them in order
connections.godot: SimHost emits signals; Battle scene plays them sequentially with Tweens and AnimationPlayer
connections.unity: SimHost raises events; BattleView queues them and plays each in a coroutine

connections.why: what happened (rounds fired, kills, loot carried, who extracted) becomes the result
connections.how: Battle keeps counters (AmmoUsed, Kills) and per-unit Carried inventory read by BattleResultBuilder
connections.godot: pure sim

godot.approach: Buttons in an action bar (HBoxContainer of Buttons) call SimHost.Battle.Do(new ShootCmd(...)); if a refusal string comes back, show it as a toast. Animations replay the event queue one at a time with Tweens; damage numbers are short-lived Label nodes.

unity.approach: A UI Toolkit action bar whose buttons build commands and pass them to SimHost; the Input System maps hotkeys to the same calls. A BattleView MonoBehaviour plays the event queue with coroutines.

newb: A command is a small object describing an intent ('unit 3 shoots unit 9'). Because it is data, the player, the AI, a replay and a test can all issue it the same way.
Refusal-first design: every command first answers 'why not?' as a sentence. The UI greys a button and shows that sentence; no duplicated rules in the UI.
Emit events, don't call the UI. The sim says 'ShotFired(hit, 14 dmg)'; the view decides how to show it. That keeps the sim testable and the presentation swappable.
Physical ammo: the magazine count is real state. Shooting spends rounds, reloading moves rounds from inventory into the gun; resolve later subtracts what was used.
pitfalls: Validating in the UI only: the AI (or a bug) then does illegal things.
Rolling the dice in a different order between runs (e.g. iterating a HashSet): breaks determinism and replays.
Teleporting a move in one go: overwatch and noticing need step-by-step movement even if the slice does not use them yet.
Letting the search window move items without weight checks, then discovering at extraction that someone carries 300 kg.
test: xUnit per command: refusals ('No line of sight.', 'No action left.'), AP and ammo spent, a forced hit with a seeded Rng deals damage in range, downed → dead after 3 turns, searched loot appears in the unit's inventory, extract removes the unit and the battle ends. Manual: play the slice raid end to end with keyboard and mouse.

title: The dead: stats & behaviour data (walker, runner)
summary: The kinds of the dead as content: hit points, speed, sight and hearing, bite damage and aim, scaled by a 'power' from the tile, plus the behaviour flags the AI reads. The slice has two: the slow walker and the fast runner.
whyHere: The AI and auto-resolve need numbers for the dead before they can chase or be fought by the numbers; it is pure data, so it is cheap and unblocks combat.ai and combat.resolve.
sliceScope: Two types in content/dead/types.json. Walker: hp 15 + 7 × power (29 at power 2), 3 tiles an action, sight 9, bite aim 55 + 3 × power, claws 12–20 × (0.6 + 0.1 × power), aware of noise. Runner: hp × 0.85, 6 tiles an action, about 15% of a mix. A spawn mix (80/20) for the slice POI. Strength value per type for auto-resolve.
fullScope: zombietypes.js + hiveconst.js ZTYPES: runners, brutes (2.4× hp, ¾ damage taken), spitters (acid), screamers (call 1–2 more), crawlers (hidden until 2.5 tiles), Bonebacks, carriers, soldier dead, sleepers, dead beasts, five counter-dead and 2 × 2 bosses; the mix widens with the years and the place (deadpool.js), each with its own turn function.

godot.approach: The defs live in the sim's ContentDb (JSON → records), not in Godot Resources, so tests see them. Godot gets only the visuals: an ArtCatalog Resource mapping art keys to SpriteFrames for an AnimatedSprite2D.

newb: Data-driven design: a new kind of dead should be a JSON entry plus (maybe) a brain, never a new class with copied stats.
A 'power' number per tile (2–10) scaling a few formulas gives you difficulty curves for free; you balance formulas, not hundreds of numbers.
Each type should ask a different answer of the player (runner: walls and overwatch; brute: heavy guns). Two types that play the same are one type too many.
Strength weights let auto-resolve treat a runner as a bit more than a walker without simulating the fight.
pitfalls: Hard-coding walker numbers inside AI code: then balancing needs a programmer.
Making the runner too fast for the slice map size: at 6 tiles an action it crosses 12 tiles a turn; check contact distance (14–20) still leaves the player one turn.
Forgetting a validation test, so a typo in brainId only shows as a crash mid-battle.
test: xUnit: walker at power 2 has 29 hp and mob 3; runner hp = round(walker hp × 0.85); mixes roll within ±2% of weights over 10 000 draws; ContentDb rejects a type with a missing brain. Manual: a debug spawn of each type shows the right figure and hover stats.

title: Enemy AI: noise, chase, attack (the dead first)
summary: How the dead (and later enemy humans) take their turns: the dead are a small state machine (unaware → investigating a noise → aware and chasing → biting) driven by sight, hearing and a shared flow field; human enemies later pick cells and targets by utility scores.
whyHere: The slice's promise is 'the dead hear and chase'; it needs pathing, LOS, actions and the dead's data, and is the last piece before a battle can be won or lost.
sliceScope: Dead FSM: Unaware (40% chance to shuffle 1–2 cells), Investigating (walk to the last noise for 3 turns, then back to Unaware), Aware (step down the flow field toward the nearest survivor, bite if adjacent). Becomes Aware on seeing a survivor within sight 9 with LOS, or hearing a noise within its radius (a shot ~ 10–15 tiles); waking one wakes its pod. All actions through the same commands as the player.
fullScope: combat.js aiUnit is a long priority list (a hand-written behaviour tree) for every side: lures, crossfire with raiders, medics, sieges, reload/unjam, flee, cover-seeking via scoreCell (high ground +2 a level, hollows −6), per-type turns (screamer hangs back and calls, brute smashes); stealth.js patrol/investigate; crossfire.js lets raiders and the dead fight; bosses register their own brains.

data: Brain ids per dead type (walker, runner) and tuning in content/ai/dead.json: shuffleChance 0.4, investigateTurns 3, podWakeAll true
Noise radii per action (gunshot by weapon, door, melee, search) and a hearing multiplier per type
Pod ids assigned at spawn (groups of 2–5 dead that wake together)

Chase: FieldCache from survivors' cells; take steps while AP and mob allow; Melee when adjacent
Human enemy brain (post-slice): score each reachable cell = cover vs visible foes + hit chance from it − exposure; pick best then best shot
Tests: a noise wakes only in-range dead and their pod; aware walker closes distance every turn; same seed → identical enemy phase

godot.approach: No Godot AI nodes needed: brains are C# classes in the sim. Godot shows only the result (walks, bites) and optional debug icons. Do not use NavigationAgent2D: it is for real-time continuous movement, not grid turns.

unity.approach: Same: brains live in the sim assembly. Avoid Unity's NavMeshAgent and visual behaviour-tree packages for this; they assume real-time and the engine. The BattleView only replays AI events.

learn.t: Game AI Pro: An Introduction to Utility Theory
Game AI Pro: The Behavior Tree Starter Kit

newb: Pick the simplest AI that is fun. The dead are mindless: a 3-4 state FSM is perfect and easy to debug. Behaviour trees shine when ordered fallbacks pile up (reload, else take cover, else flee); utility AI shines when choosing the best of many options (which cell, which target).

Utility AI = score every option with a formula and take the highest. For a raider: score each reachable cell by cover from visible foes, hit chance from there and danger; the prototype's scoreCell does exactly this.
Let the AI hear: noise is the stealth game. A gunshot wakes the dead for 10+ tiles; quiet play is rewarded, loud play brings the horde.
Pods (small groups that wake together) make the map feel alive and stop one shot waking all 40 dead.
The AI uses the same commands and rules as the player (ADR 0001 AI parity): no peeking through fog, no free moves.
pitfalls: Giving the AI omniscience (reading player positions through fog): feels unfair fast.
Iterating units or neighbours in a non-deterministic order (Dictionary, HashSet): enemy turns differ between runs and tests flake.
Dead piling into a doorway forever: when the next field step is occupied, try the second-best neighbour or wait.
Building a full behaviour-tree framework before the dead even chase: start with a switch statement.
test: xUnit: a shot at (5,5) with radius 10 wakes a walker at 8 tiles and its pod-mate at 14, not an unrelated one at 12; an aware walker's distance to the team shrinks every turn; a fixed seed reproduces the whole enemy phase event list; no brain issues a refused command. Manual: sneak past a pod, fire once, watch the pod turn and come.

title: Battle results → world, and auto-resolve
summary: The contract between the campaign and a battle: a BattleSetup goes in, a BattleResult comes out (victory / defeat / retreat, kills, the hurt and the dead, ammo used, loot), applied back to survivors, the party, the stockpile and the dead's tile count; plus fighting it 'by the numbers' when the player does not play it on the map.
whyHere: Closes the loop of the slice: without it a raid changes nothing in the world. It comes last in the lane because it reads everything the battle recorded.
sliceScope: BattleService.Start(setup) → either a played Battle or AutoResolve(setup). Result applied in one place: each unit's hp → survivor health (wounds), dead survivors removed, rounds used removed from inventories, extracted units' carried loot → party cargo (then base stockpile on return), kills → tile's dead count down. Auto-resolve: win = logistic(4.49·ln(ratio) + 3.38 vs the dead), clamped 3–97%; won: 0–half hurt for 10–40, lost: 1–all hurt for 25–75. A 'retreat' outcome if anyone extracted but not all.
fullScope: combat.js startCombat / finishCombat / autoResolveCombat: a handler registry (raid, ambush, base defence, hunt, lone attack) decides the aftermath; finishCombat also logs gunfire heat on the map, wears gear, records relations and achievements, takes prisoners, settles vehicles and tents; breakoff.js plays fights by the numbers in rounds with retreat policies (never / most / losing / blood); base defence resolves by tiers (wall, yard, buildings).

godot.approach: Keep the World in the SimHost autoload so it survives the scene change: BattleEnded → GetTree().ChangeSceneToFile("res://StateMap.tscn"). The summary screen is a Control scene reading the BattleResult; nothing about the outcome is decided in Godot code.

unity.approach: SimHost is a DontDestroyOnLoad MonoBehaviour holding the World; on BattleEnded it loads the State Map scene with SceneManager.LoadSceneAsync. The summary panel is UI Toolkit bound to the BattleResult.

newb: Treat a battle like a function call: setup in, result out. The campaign never reaches into the battle's guts, and the battle never edits the world directly; one ResultApplier does it in one place.
Handlers keyed by a string let whoever started the fight (a raid, an ambush, a base defence) decide the aftermath, without the battle knowing about any of them.

Auto-resolve is a logistic curve on the power ratio: ratio 1 is not 50/50 against the dead because the dead are worse fighters (+3.38). Tune it by playing many real battles headless and fitting the curve, as the prototype did.
Conservation tests (nothing appears or vanishes: loot out = loot that was on the map and carried out) catch the nastiest economy bugs.
pitfalls: Applying the result twice (once on 'Continue', once on load), duplicating loot: make Finish idempotent with a battle id.
Losing the World across the scene change because it lived on a scene node.
Auto-resolve that is always better than playing, so nobody plays battles: keep its wounds a bit harsher than a careful played fight.
Forgetting to subtract ammo spent, so physical ammo becomes infinite.
test: xUnit: a scripted battle result applies hp, deaths, ammo and loot exactly once; loot conservation; kills reduce the tile's dead count; AutoResolve over 10 000 seeds wins within ±2% of the formula at ratios 0.5/1/2; a save mid-battle loads to the same state hash. Manual: raid, extract with loot, see it in the stockpile at home; lose one and see the survivor gone from the roster.
